title: 1.5.12 Decompose Getting to School
description: Five multiple-choice questions on decomposition and what makes a part self-contained. Checked instantly.

questions.question: What does decomposition mean?
options: Rewriting a problem in simpler words
Removing the parts of a problem that are too hard
Breaking a complex problem into smaller parts that can be understood and solved on their own
Solving a problem the fastest way you can find
questions.explanation: Definition 1.5.2: one hard task redefined as a set of easy ones.

questions.question: The definition says the parts must be self-contained. What is the test for that?
options: Each part takes about the same amount of time
You could hand one part to someone else, with no further explanation, and get it back working
There are at least six parts
The parts are listed in the order they happen
questions.explanation: A part you can only understand while holding three others in your head has been chopped, not decomposed.

questions.question: Which of these is a genuine decomposition of "make a jam sandwich"?
options: "Open the jar": it can be understood and done on its own
"Start making it", then "finish making it"
"Make the sandwich quickly"
"Make half the sandwich", then "make the other half"
questions.explanation: Start and finish are not solvable on their own. Opening the jar is.

questions.question: You decompose "get to school on time" and one of your tasks is "get ready". Is that task finished being decomposed?
options: Yes: everyone knows what getting ready means
Yes: a task only needs breaking down if it takes over an hour
No, but only because it does not mention school
No: "get ready" hides several separate tasks, so it is not yet self-contained
questions.explanation: Wash, dress, pack the bag, eat. Each is separately doable; "get ready" is a label over the top of them.

questions.question: After listing your tasks you group them into named categories. What does grouping give you that the flat list did not?
options: It makes the list shorter
It puts the tasks into the correct time order
It exposes gaps and lopsidedness: a category with one task in it usually means you forgot something
It proves every task is self-contained
questions.explanation: The shape of the groups is information. A nearly empty category is the flat list telling you it is incomplete.
